**The Weight of Words**

Words are like feathers—light enough to carry, heavy enough to break. They drift on the wind, landing softly or striking like stones. I have 1,000 of them now, and I don’t know where to begin.

Maybe with the way the morning light slants through the blinds, turning dust into gold. Or the way my coffee smells—bitter and warm, like a memory I can’t place. Or the silence between thoughts, that vast, echoing space where everything and nothing lives.

I could write about the first time I saw the ocean. The way it stretched forever, blue and hungry, like it wanted to swallow me whole. Or the first time I realized time wasn’t a line but a spiral, looping back on itself, bringing old wounds fresh again.

Or perhaps the people. The ones who stayed, the ones who left, the ones who never existed at all. The way some voices linger in your skull long after they’ve stopped speaking. The way some hands feel like home, even when they’re gone.

I could write about fear—the cold, creeping thing that wakes you at 3 AM and whispers, *What if?* What if I’m not enough? What if I never will be? What if the world is burning and I’m just watching, holding my breath?

Or love. The kind that cracks you open, the kind that stitches you back together. The kind that makes you believe in miracles, then laughs when you do.

I could write about the books I’ve read, the songs I’ve sung, the meals I’ve cooked when I was too tired to do anything else. The way a good story can make you feel less alone, even when you’re completely, utterly by yourself.

Or the sky. Always the sky. How it changes with the hour—pink at dawn, white-hot at noon, bruised and purple at dusk. How it’s the only thing that’s always been there, watching, indifferent.

I could write about the things I’ve lost. Keys. Socks. A childhood dog who didn’t come home one night. A version of myself that no longer exists. The way grief isn’t a straight line but a maze, and you keep circling back to the same dark corners.

Or the things I’ve found. A coin on the sidewalk that made me laugh. A stranger’s smile in a crowded train. A single line of poetry that felt like a hand reaching into my chest and squeezing.

I could write about the future. The way it’s both terrifying and exciting, like standing at the edge of a cliff, knowing you have to jump but not knowing if you’ll fly or fall. The way hope is a fragile thing, easily crushed, but also impossible to kill.

Or the past. The way it’s not really gone—just folded into the present, like pages in a book you keep rereading. The way some moments feel like yesterday, even when they’re decades old.

I could write about the body. The way it aches in the morning, the way it remembers things before the mind does. The way scars tell stories, even when you don’t want them to.

Or the mind. That restless, chattering thing that never shuts up. The way it can be a prison or a palace, depending on the day.

I could write about nothing. The way the world keeps turning even when you’re not paying attention. The way the grass grows, the way the stars blink, the way time moves whether you’re ready or not.

Or everything. The way the universe is both infinite and infinitesimal, how a single cell contains the blueprint of a human, how a single human contains multitudes.

I could write about the end. The way all things must finish, the way even the longest stories have a last page. The way death is the only thing we all share, the great equalizer.

Or the beginning. The way every story starts with a breath, with a first word, with a moment of pure, unformed possibility.

I don’t know what to say. I have 1,000 words, and they feel like too many and not enough all at once. Maybe that’s the point. Words are never just words. They’re bridges, weapons, wounds, wonders. They’re the closest thing we have to magic.

So here we are. 1,000 words later, and I still don’t know where I started or where I’m going. But maybe that’s okay. Maybe the point isn’t to arrive, but to keep walking.
